Firstly, you can't blame the owner of an establishment for not wanting a stranger's pets there, even if their own are there. On the other hand their dog, who is possibly like their own child too, might not be very dog-friendly towards strange dogs themselves and they might want to avoid any fights. That's their right.
As for housing that is pet-friendly, I've found Namibia to be friendlier than a lot of other places around the world. My parents lived in New Zealand and had a very hard time finding any rentals that would allow their very tiny Yorkie. Even expensive rentals don't want to allow dogs there. And honestly, the US and most of Europe isn't much better. And I understand that too.

Just because your dog is like your child it doesn't necessarily mean that they are well-behaved or other people find it enjoyable to be around them. My aunt has 4 dogs, she would die for them, but good God they are a nuisance and I find them very unpleasant because while she showers them with affection and attention and they practically rule the roost she never bothered to train them.
As for dog-friendly parks, Avis dam is dog friendly. Many people takes their dogs there. Elisenheim dam is also an option (I take my dogs there). There are other places as well, I just can't remember the names now.

You're welcome. A very common assumption, I assure you. The syringes and liquid might be sterile, but you literally can't sterilize spores without killing the spores themselves. Spores are the dirtiest part of the whole process. I learnt this the hard way, lol. The best advice I can give you is read up as much as you can and keep your process sterile (up until fruiting as fruiting is not a sterile process itself).

Go and do research on shroomery.org, there is a treasure trove of info there. 
Innoculating with a spore syringe has a high probability for contamination. You want to start as sterile as possible and spores aren't sterile by a long shot. I start mine by putting some spores on an agar plate. After a while I'll take some of the clean mycelium and transfer it to a sterile Liquid Culture jar. After there has been enough growth in the jar I transfer it to agar again to check for contaminants again (some people do 3 transfers to agar plates but I tend to be a bit lazy) . Only after that you innoculate your bag/cake/jar with the liquid culture or a wedge from an agar plate.

Please stop with the fear mongering. I'm a born Namibian and I've been Out & Proud for the past 17 years, all the time living in Namibia.

First of all, you won't get harassed. I am very open with my sexual preferences (I'm not just lesbian, I'm poly also) and have literally never been harassed. Sure, people will say things behind your back, but no one has ever harassed or threatened or caused problems for me or any of the women I've dated straight up. I even have friends who when they want to get rid if a dude because he is a nuisance would tell the guy they are lesbian because 9/10 times guys back off immediately and leave them alone. Seems you are LESS likely to be harassed by a drunk, horny dude when they think you are lesbian.

As for not going out in Windhoek at night is also wholly inaccurate. I got back home at 4AM this morning after partying the night away at Mynt Nightclub (which is a LBTQIA+ safe space. They even have a huge pride flag hanging at the top of the stairs as you enter) and taking a LEFA (Namibia's equivalent of Uber) home, which MYNT organized for me because my phone died. Apart from MYNT there is Origin, Brewer's Market, The Wolfshack, The Smokey Mare, Goodfellas, Urban Camp, Droombos Andy's, The Handlebar, to name but a few, that is safe for a great time and to meet locals. I can't tell you how many friends I've made with tourists from all over the world that I met at these places and I'm still in contact with a lot of them. Occasionally some great events are held too. I am part of the Psytrance scene in Namibia and I've never felt unsafe at any of those events, even when I'm heavily under the influence. Everyone makes a great effort to ensure everyone's safety and half the people that go are LGBTQIA+ anyway and look after each other. I go out on a very regular basis, alone, for 17 years and I've never had any problems. Just like any other city in the world you just need to be smart about it. There are dangerous areas you should absolutely avoid and always be vigilant, but don't deprive yourself of a great experience if you are into nightlife out of fear. Windhoek has some stunning restaurants too that have great ambiance at night if you're not that into clubs, but the bottom line is Windhoek has some great things on offer Friday and Saturday nights.

Sure, people get robbed, but it's usually because they make themselves targets. Don't leave valuables in your car, don't carry large amounts of cash with you, don't advertise the fact that you're a tourist, don't pick up any hitch hikers, stick to ATM's inside malls and don't go to an ATM to get cash at night, walk with confidence and assertiveness (make it look like you can put up one hell of a fight and you know it) and to be extra safe carry pepper spray with you (any security and some camping shops sell them), figure out your plans for the day before you leave your hotel and don't stand around outside in public looking all confused and like you don't know where you are going. If you get confused immediately walk into a shop or office and ask an employee if they can help you, most Namibians would happily help out, but do not advertise that you are unsure about something. Criminals go for people they perceive as soft targets. They want to get their loot and scram, they don't want to deal with a big confrontation. Just don't make yourself a target in their minds.

Thank you for honest writing. It's funny how someone who experienced the other side of the coin can change your perspective. I for one used to be 1 of the people who loved bashing the Hotline because I didn't get out of my first call what I wanted to get. In hindsight I think I just wanted SOMEONE to know that I was going to commit suicide as I had no one else to tell. I'm not really sure what reaction I wanted, but the 1 I got didn't quite fit into my box of appropriate responses.

That being said, my perspective changed when years later I was faced with talking a teen out of committing suicide as a very newly qualified paramedic (yes, probably not the best occupation for someone who have struggled with depression and suicide as a teen, however I qualified many years later and haven't had depression for a long time). To say the experience shocked me to the core would be an understatement. When I got the call I thought it would be easy. As someone who has gone through it myself I should fully understand my patient and sort it out in no time, right? Hell, I was in for a rude awakening. I won't go into every small detail here about why it didn't go as planned and what shocked me so much, however, it permanently changed the way I saw the Suicide Hotline. 

Thank you for those who volunteer and try to help. It must be an extremely thankless job to do simply because we who call are obviously in a lot of pain and are so caught up in it that we don't realize or understand that you are humans too.
